notes: OWN QUESTION (D001) - ANSWERED IN FULL. Skin perfusion was recorded at 12 points spanning 1440 minutes (24 hours): before injection, then 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 60, 360 and 1440 minutes (methods, page 4). Tables 2, 3, 4 and 5 each report all 12 points, so the plain-ropivacaine arm (group 1) was followed to 24 hours, exactly as long as every other arm - the answer to 'was the plain-ropivacaine arm followed as long as the others' is yes. Last perfusion timepoint = 1440 min. Group 1 rose to a maximum of +160.2% at 56 min (p = 0.008), was +129.7% at 6 h (p = 0.01) and was still significantly above baseline at 24 h (+35.1%, p = 0.03). Pain was tested on a separate, shorter grid: 0, 16, 32, 48, 60, 360 and 1400 minutes (the text gives 1400 for pain against 1440 for perfusion - most likely a typo, flagged rather than relied on). Complications were followed by daily examination for 14 days. DESIGN SETTLED: prospective, randomised, double-blind (both the injected agent and the examining physician blinded), four parallel arms allocated within-subject by finger, 20 healthy volunteers, 80 fingers, 20 fingers per arm, no operation; all blocks by one physician, two-injection dorsal technique (Oberst's method) at the base of the finger. ARMS: 1 plain ropivacaine; 2 ropivacaine + epinephrine 1:1,000,000; 3 tumescent solution (ropivacaine + lidocaine + saline + epinephrine 1:1,000,000); 4 control, lidocaine 2% + 20-minute digital tourniquet. VASOCONSTRICTOR: yes, in arms 2 and 3 (epinephrine 1:1,000,000); arm 1 is plain and arm 4 has a tourniquet instead. INSTRUMENT: laser Doppler flowmetry, Perimed Master 4001 and Perimed PF2b, 780 nm, probe on the dorsal side of the finger below the nail bed (NOT the fingerpad - this matters, see F006), all fingers recorded simultaneously, 50 Hz digitisation. PAIN: needle provocation on the pulp, 1-10 VAS; average time to return of normal pain perception 6.0 h (plain ropivacaine), 18.0 h (ropivacaine + epinephrine, the longest), 8.1 h (tumescent), 4.6 h (lidocaine + tourniquet, the shortest). W-R005 JUDGED - CONFIRMED, not refuted and not narrowed. It matches population (human skin), design (any) and outcome (laser Doppler skin blood flow recorded well past 90 minutes, at 360 and 1440 min). It misses the intervention element twice over: the injection is a perineural digital nerve block at the base of the finger, not an intradermal wheal, and the flow was read at a site remote from the injection rather than at the wheal. A longer recording by a different route cannot refute a wheal-scoped claim, and the claim's wording is already explicitly wheal-limited so it is not shown too broad either. My own independent search positively supports the 90-minute figure: both human intradermal ropivacaine laser Doppler series stop at 90 minutes (Cederholm 1992 PMID 1286053, the paper's own reference [3], 'Recordings were made at 20, 40, 60, and 90 minutes after intradermal injection'; and Cederholm 1991 PMID 2038927, found by search), and the third intradermal ropivacaine study (Cederholm 1994 PMID 8067217) scored vessels by visual inspection rather than measuring flow. HAEFNER 2008: yes, the paper cites it as reference [12] and closely resembles it - same senior author (Häfner), same Tübingen department, same Oberst's-method block, same laser Doppler-to-24-hours design, 20 volunteers each. Häfner read flux at the fingerpads; Schnabl read it on the back of the finger below the nail bed. They are twin studies, which is exactly why D001's 'the one' fails. Häfner's abstract confirms every figure the D001 annotation gives for it (+155.2%, sustained vasodilatation still demonstrable at 24 h, 20 test persons). VERDICT CHANGES: D001 narrowed -> refuted (uncertain cleared); W-R005 (unjudged) -> confirmed. Unchanged but re-judged with this paper: D000 confirmed -> confirmed, D060 confirmed -> confirmed, D003 refuted -> refuted (a third instance added).
